questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

Bharath is a skilful achiever, so he __hits the nail on the leg__.

options.text: hits the nail on the head
hits the nail on the shoulder
put the nail in the hole
hits the screw on the top

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **hits the nail on the head**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The idiom "**hits the nail on the head**" is a common expression that means someone has accurately identified the main point or issue in a situation. (किसी स्थिति में मुख्य बिंदु या मुद्दे की सटीक पहचान करना)
 
• It suggests precision, correctness, or getting to the heart of the matter.
 
• It is often used when someone makes a statement or takes an action that is particularly insightful or effective.
 
 
• **Example**: *During the meeting, Sarah carefully analyzed the complex issue and, with her insightful comment, she really hit the nail on the head, identifying the root cause of the problem.*
 
 
 
• So, the correct phrase to substitute for the underlined segment "**hits the nail on the leg**" is "**hits the nail on the head**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 1**.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the following sentence.

If you do hard work, you will have the __expected results. __
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2)**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase "**desired results**" means the outcomes or results that one wants or wishes for.
 
• In the context of hard work, the results that one aims to achieve are typically the **"desired results."**
 
• The other options: "**required results**," "**good results**," and "**bad results**" do not appropriately convey the connotation of having goals or aspirations.

Therefore, the correct statement is: ***If you do hard work, you will have the desired results__.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Required results**: This implies results that are necessary, but not necessarily what one hopes for or desires.
 
• **Good results**: This is a general positive outcome but does not specify that it is what one aims for.
 
• **Bad results**: This is a negative outcome and opposite of what one would want from hard work.

**The correct sentence is:** *My uncle **has been doing**__** **business in Hyderabad for the last 10 years.*

Hence, the correct answer is** option 1.**

questions.question:
**Direction: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

She is not **__as cleverest as__** John.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **"as clever as."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase **"as clever as"** is a comparative form that indicates the same level of cleverness between two people or things.
 
• The original sentence is incorrect because** "cleverest"** is a superlative form, which means it indicates the highest degree of cleverness.
 
• The correct form to use in this sentence is** "as clever as"** because it compares the cleverness of two people.
 
• The correct answer is Option 1.

 

**Correct sentence**: *She is not **as clever as**__ John.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2, "clever"**, is not a comparative form and does not indicate any comparison between two people or things.
 
• **Option 3, "cleverest"**, is a superlative form and indicates the highest degree of cleverness, which is not appropriate for this sentence.
 
• **Option 4, "cleverer by"**, is a comparative form but is not grammatically correct without specifying what the comparison is to.

questions.question:

Neither Janki __or__ I am to receive the award.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1)**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary issue in the sentence is the incorrect conjunction "**or**" used in place of "**nor**."
 
• In the construction "neither... nor," "nor" should be used instead of "or."
 
• The correct phrase should be "**Neither Janki nor I am to receive the award**," ensuring grammatical correctness and clarity.
 
• Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

**Correct Sentence:** ***"Neither Janki nor__ I am to receive the award."***

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Neither... nor:** This pair of conjunctions is used to connect two negative alternatives.
 
• **Correct Verb Agreement:** When using "neither... nor," the verb should agree with the subject closer to the verb. In this case, "I am" is correct.
 
• **Common Mistake:** A common mistake is using "or" instead of "nor" with "neither."

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.**

Vishnu and family __are looking around into__ the possibility of moving to Canada.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **are looking into**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• Remove the preposition '**around**' to correct the sentence.
 
• Let's look at the meaning of the given phrasal verbs.
 
 
• "**Looking around**" means going through a place in order to see what is there: to explore a place.
 
• "Looking into" means trying to find out about something.
 
• "Looking upto" means to respect and admire someone.
 
 
 
• The sentence is talking about a possibility, so "**looking into**" should be used.
 
• We cannot use two prepositions (around and into) simultaneously in a single sentence. It doesn't make any sense.
 
• The implied meaning of the sentence is: Vishnu and his family are considering relocating to Canada.

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 3**, which can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

**Corrected sentence:** *Vishnu and family are looking into the possibility of moving to Canada.*

questions.question:
Select the option that will improve the given sentence by using the most appropriate pronoun.

Pradeep, whom is a teacher, also works as a content writer.

options.text: Pradeep, which is a teacher, also works as a content writer.
Pradeep, whose is a teacher, also works as a content writer.
Pradeep, who is a teacher, also works as a content writer.
Pradeep, that is a teacher, also works as a content writer.

questions.solution:
The option that will improve the given sentence by using the most appropriate pronoun is ‘3’ i.e. "Pradeep, who is a teacher, also works as a content writer."

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The correct relative pronoun to refer to a person who performs an action is **who.**

 
 
• *"Pradeep, **who **is a teacher, also works as a content writer."*
 
 
 
• The other options do not fit correctly:
 
 
• **Option 1:** which - used for things, not people.
 
• **Option 2:** whose - indicates possession.
 
• **Option 4:** that - used for things or as a restrictive clause indicator, not suitable here.
 
 

Hence, the correct answer is option 3.

questions.question:
**Direction: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.**

I have been living in this country **__since last several years__** but have never experienced any discrimination.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is** "for the last several years."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **‘since’** is used to refer to a time (an action that begun in the past and is still continuing).

 
 
• **Example**: *We have been married **since**__ 1996.*
 
 
 
• The word **‘for’ **is used to show a period of time in the past, present, or future.
 __
 
• **Example**: *I was waiting **for**__ an hour.*
 
 
 
• The phrase** "for the last several years" **is grammatically correct and means the same thing as the original sentence.
 
• The use of** "last"** indicates that the speaker is referring to a specific period of time that has already passed.
 
• Generally, when** "last"** followed by a noun, the definite article "the" is used before it.
 __
 
• **Example**: *It was **the last**__ time I won.*
 
 
 
• The correct answer is Option 1.

 

**Correct sentence**: *I have been living in this country for the last several years but have never experienced any discrimination.*

questions.question:

The doctor knew that Ravindra would recover from dengue soon and do the kind of work he __was doing__ before.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: "**had been doing**".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 

__
 
• The sentence is in the past tense, indicating that the doctor already knew something before.
 
• "**Had been doing**" is the **past perfect continuous tense**, indicating that Ravindra was doing a certain kind of work before he got sick.
 
• The structure should be: Subject + had been + present participle (verb + ing)__
 
• This tense is appropriate because it shows that Ravindra was doing the work for a period of time before he got sick and that he may continue doing it after he recovers.
 
• The use of "**had been doing**" implies a continuous action or state in the past, emphasizing the ongoing nature of the work. 

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 4**.

**Corrected sentence**: *The doctor knew that Ravindra would recover from dengue soon and do the kind of work he had been doing before.*

• Must expresses obligation or compulsion imposed by the speaker.
 
• Whereas 'have to' expresses external obligations.
 
 
 
• Example:

• *They have to help the needy. (others think this and not the speaker)*
